summary:
Amos came from "among the sheepherders of Tekoa" (1:1), a village in Judah south of Jerusalem, but he was sent north to the separate kingdom of Israel. He spoke "two years before the earthquake" (1:1), a quake remembered centuries later (Zechariah 14:5), under Uzziah of Judah and Jeroboam II of Israel in the mid-700s BC. Jeroboam's long reign had expanded Israel's borders (2 Kings 14:25), and the book's targets live off the results: "beds inlaid with ivory" (6:4) — ivory inlays have been excavated at Samaria, the northern capital — and "wine by the bowlful" (6:6). Within a few decades Assyria destroyed Samaria and deported Israel (722 BC; 2 Kings 17).

The book opens with oracles (spoken judgments from God) against Israel's neighbors — Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Edom, Ammon, Moab, then Judah — each beginning like the first: "For three transgressions of Damascus, even four, I will not revoke My judgment" (1:3). The eighth is Israel itself: "they sell the righteous for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals" (2:6). Chapters 3–6 detail bribes, grain exacted from the poor, and justice denied at the city gate, where courts were held (5:10–12). Chosenness is no shelter: "Only you have I known from all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities" (3:2). God refuses the feasts, "I hate, I despise your feasts!" (5:21), and asks instead, "But let justice roll on like a river, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream" (5:24). Israel longed for the Day of the LORD, the day God comes to judge; Amos turns it around: "It will be darkness and not light" (5:18).

Chapters 7–9 record five visions. At the first two, locusts and fire, Amos intercedes and God relents. At the third, God sets a plumb line (a builder's cord for testing that a wall is straight) against Israel: "I will no longer spare them" (7:8). The fourth is a Hebrew pun: a basket of summer fruit (qayits) announces the end (qets) — "The end has come for My people Israel" (8:2). Between the visions, Amaziah the priest of Bethel reports Amos for conspiracy and orders him home: "never prophesy at Bethel again, because it is the sanctuary of the king" (7:13). Amos answers, "I was not a prophet, nor was I the son of a prophet; rather, I was a herdsman and a tender of sycamore-fig trees" (7:14).

The final vision has the Lord beside the altar, commanding a judgment none escape (9:1–4), then a leveling question: "Are you not like the Cushites to Me, O children of Israel?" (9:7) — a people far up the Nile — for God has moved other nations too, Philistines from Caphtor, Arameans from Kir. The book ends in restoration: "Yet I will not utterly destroy the house of Jacob" (9:8); "In that day I will restore the fallen tent of David" (9:11), with rebuilt cities, replanted vineyards, and nations that bear God's name. James quotes Amos 9:11–12 at the Jerusalem council to argue that Gentile believers belong among God's people (Acts 15:16–17).
